raw_case_text:
A 64-year-old Egyptian gentleman residing in Qatar, he has a long-standing history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy with a low ejection fraction (LV EF 26%), underwent implantation of a cardiac resynchronization therapy device (CRT-D) in 2013. Two years later, the CRT-D was downgraded to ICD.
On February 11th, 2020, the patient suffered from an ischemic stroke in the right middle cerebral artery for which he required decompressive craniectomy. Shortly after the procedure, his hospital stay was complicated with fever and malaise. Ingestion of partially boiled cow's milk was noted from the history. Blood cultures were positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Brucella melitensis. Based on these results, he was diagnosed with pneumonia and brucellosis, and antibiotics were commenced for treatment. As a result of the stroke, the patient suffered from hemiplegia which left him bed-bound and shifted to a rehabilitation centre for continuity of care. There, the patient showed only minor improvements in speech, but none in mobility. Nevertheless, the family refused to transfer him to a multispecialty hospital that provides medical, surgical, and long-term care.
On November 20th, 2020, while the patient was still in the rehabilitation centre, his health started to deteriorate. He was found to be hypotensive with a blood pressure of 80/40, but afebrile with an oral temperature of 37.0 C. His heart rate and respiratory rate were 93 beats/minute and 18 breaths/minute, respectively. Physical examination revealed no skin changes over the ICD pocket, no cardiac murmurs on auscultation, and no apparent localized signs of infection. Blood tests revealed a normal white blood cell count (5 x 103 cells/mm3) and high C-reactive protein level (77 mg/L). Blood cultures were positive for Brucella melitensis. These tests were followed with transthoracic echocardiography which showed a single oscillating mass measuring 0.8 x 0.4 cm attached to the tip of the right atrial lead of the ICD suggestive of vegetation (Figure 1).
The patient was then transferred to the Heart Hospital as a case of relapsing brucellosis with brucella endocarditis and ICD-lead colonization. The Infectious Disease Team was consulted, and three-drug regimen was commenced including rifampicin (600 mg/day), gentamicin (5 mg/kg/day), and doxycycline (200 mg/day). Gentamicin was then increased to 7 mg/kg/day as the postdose peak levels were low, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (960 mg/12 h) was added to the treatment, with a recommendation to remove the ICD. A transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) was tried but was technically difficult to conduct due to the restricted neck movements and limited jaw mobility of the patient, which rendered the TEE probe impossible to insert. Therefore, a positron emission tomography (PET) scan was performed to confirm the nature of the vegetation, yet the results were being inconclusive.
The case was discussed in a multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting, and all possibilities to deal with this infected ICD wires were explored. Due to the unavailability of laser-assisted lead extraction, surgery was proposed as an option; however, because of the patient's general condition, surgical removal was considered a high-risk procedure, and the final decision was to keep the ICD in place and to treat him conservatively with antibiotics. Another PET scan was requested that was also inconclusive, and a repeated echocardiogram revealed a slight increase in vegetative size (0.8 x 0.6 cm). Eventually, Gentamicin was stopped due to renal impairment.
On December 17th, 2020, the patient was medically fit for discharge and was sent home with oral antibiotics for 6 weeks.
On March 29th, 2021, the patient was doing well and still on oral antibiotics.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old male residing in a rehabilitation center presented with acute clinical deterioration and hypotension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had a history of ischemic stroke in February 2020 requiring decompressive craniectomy, complicated by post-procedural fever and bacteremia requiring antibiotics, leaving him with residual left hemiplegia and bed-bound in a rehabilitation center. On November 20, 2020, his condition deteriorated acutely with marked hypotension and systemic decline. Transthoracic echocardiography identified a right atrial lead vegetation. He was transferred to a cardiac hospital for medical management and antimicrobial therapy, achieving clinical stability by December 17, 2020.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction 26%), CRT-D implantation in 2013 downgraded to ICD in 2015; right MCA ischemic stroke status post decompressive craniectomy in February 2020 complicated by Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia and hemiplegia. Epidemiological exposure: History of consuming partially boiled cow's milk.
subjective.review_of_systems: Malaise, speech impairment, limited mobility, and restricted neck and jaw movement. Home medications and allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Vitals: Blood pressure 80/40 mmHg, oral temperature 37.0 °C (afebrile), heart rate 93 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. Exam: No erythema or skin changes over the ICD pocket, no cardiac murmurs on auscultation, no localized signs of infection. Neurological: Residual hemiplegia, restricted neck movements, and limited jaw mobility.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: White blood cell count 5 x 10^3 cells/mm^3 (normal), C-reactive protein (CRP) 77 mg/L (elevated). Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE): Single oscillating mass measuring 0.8 x 0.4 cm attached to the tip of the right atrial lead of the ICD, suggestive of vegetation. Repeat echocardiogram: Slight increase in vegetation size to 0.8 x 0.6 cm. Later labs: Developed renal impairment during aminoglycoside therapy.
objective.advanced_workup: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE): Attempted, but technically unsuccessful due to restricted neck movements and limited jaw mobility preventing probe insertion. Positron emission tomography (PET) scan: Performed twice to characterize the lead vegetation; both scans were inconclusive.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Relapsing Brucellosis with Brucella endocarditis and ICD-lead colonization, confirmed by blood cultures positive for Brucella melitensis (as well as prior positive blood cultures for B. melitensis and Streptococcus pneumoniae in February 2020 following raw milk ingestion).
Plan & Clinical Course: Multidisciplinary team recommended ICD removal, but laser extraction was unavailable and open surgical extraction carried prohibitively high operative risk; managed conservatively with medical therapy. Triple regimen initiated: rifampicin 600 mg/day, gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day (later increased to 7 mg/kg/day based on low peak levels), and doxycycline 200 mg/day, with addition of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 960 mg every 12 hours. Gentamicin was subsequently discontinued due to nephrotoxicity. The patient improved, was deemed fit for discharge on December 17, 2020 on oral antibiotics for 6 weeks, and remained well on oral therapy at follow-up on March 29, 2021.
